openings.claim: The shelving organization may manufacture part of its own retrieval demand: moving arrivals into surname order makes the pre-opening exception slip stale, causing second-location searches and pressure for further shelving or corrections. The supplied synthetic observations support testing this feedback path, not an established effect.
openings.delta: Remove the relocation link for a bounded batch already on the existing cart: keep its location stable through the evening window instead of shelving it during that window. Preserve the clerk's reader verification and correct-hold delivery.
openings.prediction: For comparable arrival size and desk congestion, the stationary batch will have fewer stale exception entries and second-location searches than batches moved after the slip was written, improving the fraction finishing within two minutes without wrong-reader handoffs.
openings.rival_prediction: The cart sample may contain unusually easy pickups, while independent recording errors or household-name mismatches drive delays. Under that alternative, matching book size and arrival mix will erase the cart advantage, and keeping locations stationary will not materially reduce second searches.
openings.defeat: Verified stationary batch locations still produce equally frequent stale entries and second searches, or matched pickups remain equally slow; any wrong-reader handoff defeats the proposed intervention's required outcome.
openings.probe: Across bounded matched evening samples, use only books already fitting on the cart; defer their shelving until the window ends and keep their exception entries behind the desk. The existing clerk records movement, second searches, pickup times and handoff errors on the existing timing sheet. Count all daily preparation, including probe setup, against ten clerk-minutes. Compare stationary and usual-movement samples while recording arrival mix and congestion; assess the 95% target separately from evidence for the feedback path.
